claims.claim: In 2024, Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1: Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 (title, authors, publisher abstract, online 2024-08-14, Nature 632:570-575); full text of PMC11324516 read as passages via Firecrawl research read_paper
claims.note: Title: 'A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge'. Abstract: 'remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'. Body: isotopic data 'indicate that the Altar Stone of Stonehenge has a provenance from the ORS in the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland'. Published 14 Aug 2024. The date frames it as the 2024 finding.

claims.claim: Now nobody can say exactly where it came from.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (publisher abstract, online 2026-11-05); Crossref works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (publisher abstract, online 2026-06-04); doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full-text PDF from https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/3293/galley/18572/download/ (p.129)
claims.note: Pirrie 2026: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'. Clarke 2026: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. Literally true. Only the abstracts of the two 2026 papers were read. Pedant risk: Parker Pearson 2024 p.129 already said 'As yet, the actual outcrop from which the Altar Stone was extracted is unknown', so the exact spot was never known; 'Now' is true as 'as of now', not as 'no longer'. Acceptable because the line contrasts 'traced to Scotland' with 'exactly', and the 2024 line never claimed an exact spot.

claims.claim: (A4) What the hook leaves a viewer who swipes away: at second two, 'scientists traced the Altar Stone to Scotland in 2024'; after the second sentence, 'that answer has since become less certain and the exact source is unknown'.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 Crossref abstract and PMC11324516 passages; Crossref abstracts of doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090 and doi:10.1002/jqs.70080
claims.note: Second-two belief is true (claim 1). The second belief is supported by Pirrie 2026's abstract, which includes three of the 2024 authors: many Orcadian Basin ORS outcrops 'could not have been the source', no examined UK ORS outcrop area 'can be shown' to match, and it cites the 2024 grain dating only as supporting 'a Laurentian source for the heavy minerals' rather than the Orcadian Basin specifically. The hook does not say the stone is not from Scotland, which neither 2026 paper says (Clarke 2026 still gives Caithness as 'the closest match in zircon age structure'). Only abstracts of the 2026 papers were read.

claims.claim: The ages of tiny mineral grains inside it matched sandstone in the northeast.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text (PMC11324516 passages via Firecrawl research read_paper); Crossref abstract of doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1
claims.note: Abstract: 'the age and chemistry of detrital zircon, apatite and rutile grains from within fragments of the Altar Stone' and the Orcadian Basin 'remarkable similarity'. Tiny: heavy-mineral grains 'typically 10-40 um wide'; zircon targets 'usually <30 um in width'. Matched: Orcadian Basin zircon spectra give 'the closest match'; Kolmogorov-Smirnov 'fails to reject the null hypothesis that they are derived from the same underlying distribution'; apatite U-Pb components from Spittal (Caithness) and Cruaday (Orkney) 'match those from the Altar Stone'. 'Inside it' = fragments attributed to the stone (direct sampling not permitted), which is what 'from within fragments' says. The zircon ages are equally indistinguishable from Svalbard ORS and the Laurentian basement; the line says 'matched', not 'matched only', so it holds.

claims.claim: If so, how did six tonnes travel more than seven hundred kilometres?
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 Crossref abstract and PMC11324516 passages; doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 PDF (abstract p.113, p.117); Crossref abstract of doi:10.1002/jqs.70080
claims.note: Clarke 2024 abstract: 'Such a provenance implies that the Altar Stone, a 6 tonne shaped block, was sourced at least 750 km from its current location'; body: 'a Scottish provenance ... demands a transport distance of at least 750 km'. Parker Pearson 2024 abstract: 'northern Scotland more than 700 km away', 'The six-tonne Altar Stone'. Clarke 2026: 'the 6000 kg central sandstone megalith', 'some 700 km away'. 'If so' keeps the sources' condition (distance holds for an Orcadian Basin source). No date is given, consistent with Parker Pearson p.117 'Just when the Altar Stone arrived at Stonehenge is unknown'.

claims.claim: The 2024 team suggested it went by sea.
claims.note: Abstract: 'The difficulty of long-distance overland transport of such massive cargo from Scotland, navigating topographic barriers, suggests that it was transported by sea.' Body: sea routes southward 'would have permitted'. 'Suggested' keeps the hedge.

claims.claim: But no late Stone Age boat has been found in Britain,
claims.source_checked: doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 full-text PDF (UCL Press; 'Published: 31 December 2024'; states double-blind peer review; CC BY 4.0), p.128
claims.note: p.128: 'Although no boats are known from the Late Neolithic in Britain or Europe'; 'The earliest known boats in Britain have been found ... at Ferriby. The earliest of these Early Bronze Age sewn-plank boats (Ferriby 3) dates to 2030-1780 cal bc'. 'Late Stone Age' = Late Neolithic (Neolithic is the New Stone Age); 'Britain' is narrower than the source's 'Britain or Europe'.

claims.claim: and another study doubts one could carry six tonnes.
claims.note: p.128: 'What we know of Early Bronze Age boats ... would suggest that they and their Late Neolithic precursors were unlikely to be sturdy enough to carry a 6-tonne stone in coastal waters'; a sewn-plank boat for 6 t 'would have to be far greater than the estimated 15 m-16 m length of the Ferriby boats'. 'Doubts' = 'unlikely'. Note, not a fault: 'another study' is not independent of the 2024 team, as Bevins, Ixer and Pearce co-wrote both; the script flags shared authors only for the later study (claim 11).

claims.claim: Overland, on a sledge, that study estimates about eight months of hauling.
claims.note: p.128: 'a suitably robust wooden sledge with vegetation-made shock absorbers, sliding on wooden rails'; 'we might calculate that such a journey with a large and heavy sledge could take perhaps four times today's time of under two months ... needing eight months or so to haul a stone from northern Scotland to Stonehenge.' 'Estimates about' matches 'might calculate ... perhaps ... or so'; it is a rough back-of-envelope figure, which 'about' conveys.

claims.claim: A glacier? A 2026 ice model says ice could have carried it part of the way, at most.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (publisher-deposited abstract, online 2026-06-04, J. Quat. Sci. 41:888-895). ONLY THE ABSTRACT WAS READ; Wiley full text not opened.
claims.note: Abstract: 'Proposed mechanisms include ... southward movement as a glacial erratic'; 'we combine sandstone provenance analysis with ice flow modelling'; 'Glacial dispersal to Dogger Bank would reduce the anthropogenic transport distance required to Stonehenge from 700 km to 400 km'; 'Glacial transport may have provided an intermediate stage in the stone's journey, but alone cannot account for the final emplacement on Salisbury Plain. Even under a glacially assisted scenario, substantial anthropogenic transport would have remained necessary.' 'Could have ... part of the way, at most' does not exceed 'may have provided an intermediate stage'. The abstract's further timing problem (Dogger Bank inundated before the stone likely arrived) only weakens the glacier case, so 'at most' still holds.

claims.claim: Then, months later, a new study, including three of the 2024 team, looked closer.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (authors, online 2026-11-05, abstract); Crossref works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (online 2026-06-04); Crossref works/10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 (authors)
claims.note: Pirrie 2026 published online 5 Nov 2026, five months after the ice-model paper (4 Jun 2026). Clarke 2024 authors: Clarke, Kirkland, Bevins, Pearce, Glorie, Ixer. Pirrie 2026 authors include Richard E. Bevins, Rob A. Ixer and Nick J. G. Pearce and none of the other three: exactly three. 'Looked closer' = abstract's 'a detailed multi-proxy characterization of the sedimentology, geochemistry, detrital and diagenetic mineralogy of the Altar Stone'. Abstract only.

claims.claim: Many outcrops in that part of Scotland could not have been the source.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (publisher-deposited abstract). ONLY THE ABSTRACT WAS READ; Lyell Collection full text not opened.
claims.note: Abstract: 'the overall petrology, heavy mineral assemblage, clay mineralogy and geochemistry show that many outcrops of the Old Red Sandstone (ORS) in the Orcadian Basin could not have been the source of the Altar Stone.' 'That part of Scotland' = the northeast (claim 4), i.e. the Orcadian Basin of NE Scotland (Clarke 2024; Parker Pearson 2024 abstract describes its extent from Orkney and Shetland to Inverness and Banff).

claims.claim: No outcrop examined so far has been shown to match it in every way.
claims.source_checked: Crossref works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (publisher-deposited abstract); Crossref works/10.1002/jqs.70080 (abstract). ONLY ABSTRACTS WERE READ.
claims.note: Pirrie 2026: 'To date, no examined outcrop area of the UK ORS can be shown to have the same suite of lithological and geochemical characteristics as documented for the Altar Stone.' 'So far' = 'To date'; 'has been shown to' = 'can be shown to'; 'in every way' = 'the same suite of ... characteristics'. The script drops 'of the UK ORS', which makes it read as the examined outcrops only; Clarke 2026 ('closest match' in zircon age structure, source 'unresolved') reports no full match either. Consistent with claim 4, which is limited to grain ages.
